newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North Korean defector is now a marked man.
newsitem.headline: North Korean defector is now a marked man.

text.p: North Korea's top ideologue found temporary refuge in the Philippines on Tuesday, but he is now a marked man -- a traitor forever dogged by fear of Pyongyang hitmen.
Hwang Jang-yop got a warning just three days after seeking asylum in Beijing when a prominent North Korean defector was fatally shot near Seoul.
The victim, Li Il-nam, was a nephew of the former wife of North Korean leader Kim Jong-il.
Li was so terrified Kim would exact revenge he underwent plastic surgery on his face, changed his name and restlessly moved from one address to another.
But his cover was blown by a local magazine, and on February 15 two suspected Pyongyang agents hunted him down. He was shot through the head with a Czech-made pistol outside a friend's apartment.
China took the security threat seriously. As an old socialist comrade of the North and an ally in the 1950-53 Korean War, it has unique inside knowledge of Pyongyang's unpredictable moods and rages.

Beijing was so nervous as Hwang languished for five weeks in a South Korean diplomatic mission that it stationed armoured personnel carriers outside the compound, deployed police armed with assault rifles in the area and blocked approaches with tyre-shredding spikes.
South Korean diplomats reported several attempts by North Koreans to break into the building.
North Koreans in parked cars near the consulate fuelled the tension.
On Tuesday a Seoul foreign ministry official sought to reasssure South Koreans that Hwang was "secure and safe" in a third country.
But even when he reaches Seoul, his security will never be completely assured.
North Korea has a history of deadly attacks against its arch-rival South Korea. The two Koreas are still frozen in Cold War confrontation.

In 1983, North Korean assassins planted a bomb in Rangoon that killed 21 people, including four South Korean government ministers. The blast was intended to kill then South Korean president Chun Doo Hwan, who escaped unharmed.
Four years later a bomb planted by a North Korean female agent blew up a Korean Air Lines Boeing 707 above the Andaman Sea, killing all 115 people on board.

Among other atrocities, 31 armed communist agents infiltrated almost to the gates of Seoul's presidential Blue House in 1968. Twenty eight intruders were killed in a gunbattle in which 34 South Koreans also died.

Two days later, a U.S. navy vessel, the Pueblo, with 84 seamen aboard was seized by North Korea in international waters off the Korean peninsula's east coast. Almost 11 months later, 82 crew members were released.

More recently, a North Korean submarine landed 26 armed commandos on a Southern beach last September, sparking a huge manhunt in which 24 infiltrators were shot dead. One was captured alive and one evaded the dragnet.
Along the heavily-fortified Korean border, there have been numerous deadly flare-ups.
The most gruesome incident occurred in 1976 when two U.S. military officers pruning a tree in the border truce village of Panmunjom were axed to death by People's Army soldiers.
